title: Universal free school meals
headline: A free lunch for every pupil. About £2.2bn a year.
description: Extend free school meals to every pupil in a state-funded school in England. Most of the way there already: infants get a free meal automatically, and from September 2026 every child in a household on universal credit qualifies. The cost here is the pupils who are still left out, about 4.4 million of them, funded at the department's own rate of £505 a pupil a year.

baselinePolicy.text: Free school meals in England were extended from the 2026/27 academic year to every child in a household on universal credit, funded with over £1bn across the Spending Review period. Infants already get a free meal under universal infant free school meals.
alreadyIncludes: Free school meals for all children in households receiving universal credit from September 2026 (over £1bn across 2026 to 2029).
Universal infant free school meals for reception, year 1 and year 2.

source.note: pupil numbers and free school meal eligibility, January 2026 census

terms.label: Pupils in state-funded schools with no free meal today

source.note: 8.355m state-funded pupils, less 2.214m eligible on the benefits criteria, less about 0.5m added by the universal credit expansion, less the 1.2m infants covered by universal infant free school meals

terms.label: Schools funding for a free meal, a pupil a year

source.quote: each meal taken by an eligible pupil attracts £2.66. An allocation assumes that pupils will take 190 school meals over an academic year, providing £505 per eligible pupil

rawSource.note: Pupils not already entitled, times the department's own funding rate. Nobody has costed universal free school meals officially; this is our arithmetic on two published figures.

caveats: The 0.5m added by the universal credit expansion is the government's own "over half a million more children", not a measured figure: the first census to capture the expansion is October 2026. Some of those children are infants already counted under universal infant free school meals, so subtracting both groups separately makes this figure, if anything, too low.
This funds a place, not a meal eaten. Only 80% of eligible pupils took a meal on census day and 88% of infants did, so meals actually served would cost less than the funding shown.
Held flat in cash. In practice the meal rate rises each year while pupil numbers are falling, about 1.2% last year, and the two partly offset.

considerations.text: A universal entitlement removes the means test, and with it the registration gap: a fifth of pupils already entitled to a free meal did not take one on census day.

This reaches 4.4 million families who currently pay for lunch, most of them above the universal credit line but not wealthy. It also pays for the lunches of the well off, which is the usual objection to universality.
These are English pupils. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland set their own school meal policies and would receive Barnett consequentials on top of the figure shown.
